spatial_claims.claim: A is a cone/cylinder with base diameter d_A and height h_A; B is similar with base diameter d_B and height h_B; similarity gives d_A:d_B = h_A:h_B
Construct solid C with same base as A (diameter d_A) and same height as B (height h_B)
C and B have the same height h_B, so by 12.11 their ratio equals the ratio of their bases
A and C share the same base circle of diameter d_A; inscribed prisms with regular polygonal bases approximate the cylinders
Cyl_A and Cyl_C share the same base as their respective cones A and C

configuration_map: Three solids in the configuration: A (base diameter d_A, height h_A), B (base diameter d_B, height h_B), and auxiliary solid C (base diameter d_A, height h_B). C is constructed to share one dimension with each of A and B: it has A's base and B's height. This allows comparison A:C via equal bases (ratio of heights) and C:B via equal heights (ratio of bases). The similarity condition d_A:d_B = h_A:h_B links the two comparisons. No complex spatial positioning is involved - only dimensional relationships between solids.
pass_reason: The proof is predominantly proportional/algebraic. Its spatial claims are limited to dimensional relationships between three solids (shared bases and heights) which are all mutually consistent. There are no angle decompositions, point-inside-figure claims, ray orderings, or complex spatial arrangements that could produce configuration contradictions.
